newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: China battles to satisfy diesel demand.
newsitem.headline: China battles to satisfy diesel demand.

text.p: China's struggle to keep pace with the rampant demand for diesel fuel could extend well into 1997 as it battles to satisfy the agricultural, transport and power generation sectors, industry officials said.
High import prices for crude and oil products through most of 1996 prompted China to limit imports, sparking sharp demand on stocks and a shortage by the end of the year.
The country's infrastructure, where diesel has to compete with other commodities for space on the all-important railway network, was struggling to keep pace.
And analysts predicted generally high import prices for 1997, so shortages could occur well into this year.

"Supply will still lag behind demand this year and we may risk having a similar oil shortage situation so long as Sinopec refineries are not upgraded fast enough and transport infrastructure are still bad," one Sinopec source said.
"Unless key infrastructure are in place, we would always be susceptible to import irregularities, in particular when international spot prices are high," the source said.
Like other expanding Asian economies in 1996, China broiled under the heat of the highest international crude and product prices in five years.
Diesel in Singapore hit a five-year high of $34.15 per barrel in December. On Monday, gas oil was valued at $30.70, but still seven dollars per barrel higher than a year-earlier.

Latest customs figures show that by November 1996, China had imported just four million tonnes of diesel, or a monthly average 363,000 tonnes. But with a growing shortage, China is to import one million tonnes of diesel in January to fill the gap, officials said earlier this month.
"The government had allowed for a total import volume of close to seven million tonnes of diesel in 1996," a Sinopec source said.
"In December, the high international prices caused us to curb imports, despite depleting domestic inventories, as they were too expensive," a Sinopec source said.

China also raised the domestic price of diesel twice in the fourth quarter to try to ease the burden on refiners, and promoted greater diesel output domestically. Diesel production rose 11 percent in 1996 to 43.25 million tonnes.

China watchers said the government was likely to try to avoid shortages in 1997 as much as possible as it comes under the world's spotlight. Five-yearly Congress elections are under way and China takes over sovereignty of Hong Kong at the end of June.

But Chinese sources said the demand for diesel was still rising, especially in the high consumption cities and industrial areas in southern Guangdong province, so further shortages could occur, especially if import prices remain high in 1997.

Diesel demand for cars has been rising at an "alarming rate", a Sinopec source said. In recent years, more cars have switched to diesel as its price has become more competitive with that of gasoline. Agricultural demand is rising at 3-4 percent a year.
The switch to more diesel output also prompted many power companies to use more diesel instead of fuel oil, adding to the demand.
